![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/12acb33aa174f1c174a538a89881dd19245f733c6b39df37f9ebbdc1f86442d5.png)

Consider the region $D$ shown above. If $R=[-3,1]\times [-1,2],$ and

$$
{∬}_{D}({2}^{x}-y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of $f(x,y)?$

I. $\{\begin{aligned}{2}^{x}-y, & (x,y)\in R \\ 0, & (x,y)\notin R\end{aligned}$

II. $\{\begin{aligned}{2}^{x}-y, & (x,y)\in R∖D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in D\end{aligned}$

III. $\{\begin{aligned}{2}^{x}-y, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our region $D$ and rectangle $R:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/56f6557f98674b0f651a781e6226ba9d207273e30136e3396c3aabcf91a64024.png)

Notice that the rectangle $R$ contains the region $D$ completely. 

Now, if we define $f(x,y)$ to be equal ${2}^{x}-y$ on $D$ and to be equal $0$ outside $D,$ we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}({2}^{x}-y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given functions.

- We cannot use functions I and II. Both of these functions are not identically zero for all points in $R∖D.$ For example, $(x,y)=(1,0)\in R∖D$, but the functions are nonzero at this point.

- Function III equals ${2}^{x}-y$ on $D$ and equals $0$ outside $D.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
